item.title: Small nations don’t need a Space Force. They need the right space organization.
item.description: The establishment of the United States Space Force, China’s Aerospace Force and France’s Space Command has prompted political and military leaders to consider creating similar organizations. For small and medium-sized states, that temptation is a trap. Recognizing space as a warfighting domain compels smaller states to develop military space organizations — but not as national symbols. The main limitations are the strategic position of these small states and their budgets to build and sustain such organizations. For small and medium-sized states, creating a military space organization involves an opportunity cost. Resources could alternatively be allocated to building more combat units or acquiring additional tanks, aircraft and ships. On the other hand, a smaller military space organization may be a force multiplier to help the mission.

item.title: With the proliferation of European satellites, we need a new approach to space-based surveillance
item.description: European space companies are expanding rapidly. They are attracting substantial investment, developing new satellite services and competing for contracts once reserved for large aerospace groups. But as more satellites enter low Earth orbit (LEO), operators face a growing problem: how can they monitor and protect the spacecraft on which communications, navigation, financial transactions and national security increasingly depend?
